Protect the Home page from promotional overload: because prominent links reliably boost traffic, every stakeholder competes for space in a tragedy of the commons, so resist over-promoting, educate stakeholders about the shared cost of clutter, and offer alternative ways to drive traffic.

Treat the first few seconds as critical (the Big Bang effect): users form reliable snap judgments in milliseconds and force-fit later information onto a first (possibly wrong) impression, so orient them correctly from the start, and because many arrive on deep pages, let every page convey who you are and what you offer.

State clearly what the site is: provide a tagline by the Site ID (clear, ~six-to-eight words, differentiating, a value proposition not a motto), a terse prominent Welcome blurb, and a 'Learn more' option; use as much space as needed but no more, never a mission statement, and usability-test this with outsiders because insiders will not notice the main point is missing.

Do not settle usability disputes by opinion: web teams waste time in unresolvable 'religious debates' because members project their own personal and professional preferences onto users and assume most people are like them.

Reject the myth of the average user (web use is idiosyncratic and there is no simple right answer to important design questions) and resolve disputes by testing rather than opinion: replace 'do people like X?' with 'does this specific thing work for the people likely to use it?', because testing shifts discussion from opinion to what actually works.

Act as a user advocate, never a manipulator: serve users' real needs, treat persuasion as acceptable only when it is not deceptive, refuse dark patterns and manipulation because that is not your job, and do not use usability tests to judge desirability (a market-research question).

Test with real users because you cannot see your own site freshly: any testing beats none, testing one user early beats fifty near the end, and problems should be caught early since changing a live site is hard.

Make testing cheap and habitual: do it yourself when time and money are short, test about three users one morning a month on a fixed recurring day, keep it simple so you keep doing it, prefer more rounds over exhaustive ones, and use remote or unmoderated testing to widen the participant pool.

Treat do-it-yourself testing as qualitative, not proof: about three participants per round is enough, the goal is actionable insight, and since you will always find more problems than you can fix you must focus on the most serious ones.

Interpret test results wisely: do not over-react to individual aesthetic or color reactions, recognize the three recurring problem types (unclear concept, missing words, too much going on), ignore recoverable 'kayak' problems, and treat participants' new-feature requests with skepticism.

Debrief immediately and triage ruthlessly: fix the most serious problems first via a collective list, top-ten selection, ranking, and an ordered fix list with owners; fix only enough to declassify each serious problem then stop; keep a separate low-hanging-fruit list; and prefer removing what obscures meaning over adding explanations.

Design mobile around good tradeoffs: the same usability principles apply (users move even faster and read even less), design is fundamentally constraints and tradeoffs, most serious usability problems stem from tradeoffs that underweight the user, so use Mobile First to identify essentials and do not assume mobile users only want 'on the move' features.

Manage small-screen space by prioritizing rather than sacrificing usability: keep frequent or urgent things close at hand, accept more tapping and scrolling as long as the scent of information stays strong, never trade away usability to fit the space, use responsive design rather than maintaining separate site versions, and honor mobile courtesies (allow zooming, deep-link to the actual content, and offer a full-site option).

Keep affordances visible: treat them as the visual clues that signal how to use something (clearer cues give a clearer signal), make the ones users need noticeable and never hide them, replace hover-dependent features because touch screens have no cursor, and when using flat design compensate for the distinctions it removes with the remaining visual dimensions.

Prioritize speed, because slow performance frustrates users and loses goodwill (especially on mobile, where download speeds are unreliable), so avoid loading more code or larger images than the user's screen needs.

Make products learnable, memorable, and appropriately delightful: center effort on learnability, effectiveness, and efficiency (leaving 'useful' and 'desirable' to pre-project market research), make things easy to learn the first time so they are easy to relearn, and add delight to compete without sacrificing usability.

Test mobile with the same process as desktop and solve only the logistics: use a camera pointed at or attached to the device so observers can see gestures, let users hold the device naturally, and skip the distracting face camera.

Treat usability as courtesy by managing the user's goodwill reservoir: beyond being clear, behave considerately, and remember every user arrives with a limited, idiosyncratic, situational, refillable reserve of goodwill that each problem drains and a single bad mistake can empty.

Increase goodwill by serving users well: make the main tasks obvious and easy, be candid about things you would rather hide, save users steps and visibly put effort in, answer likely questions with genuine up-to-date FAQs, make errors easy to recover from, and apologize when you cannot do what a user wants.

Build accessibility in, starting with clarity: a site is not usable unless it is accessible (and it is simply the right thing to do), the most effective step is fixing what confuses everyone (fixing code without clarity does not help), design for screen-reader users who 'scan with their ears' by front-loading link and heading text, and implement the high-impact basics (alt text, correct headings, labeled forms, a skip link, keyboard access, strong contrast, an accessible template).

Bootstrap organizational support pragmatically: run your first test on your own time (simple, free, with a visible quick win), test competitors' sites as a low-risk way to build interest, and approach management with genuine empathy and humility, sharing what you know rather than preaching.

Honor the few hard rules that always apply: never use small, low-contrast type; do not put labels inside form fields unless strict safeguards all hold; and preserve the browser's distinction between visited and unvisited text links.

Treat all this guidance as principles you may knowingly bend or break: there are even cases where you deliberately want the interface to make people think, provided you know which rule you are bending and believe you have a good reason.
Match the chatbot's communication style to its target audience and domain to support user satisfaction.

Treat the chatbot's domain and context as an indirect moderator - the same practice can help in one domain and hurt in another - and tune target impacts to the domain (health toward well-being, mental-health toward closeness and trust, commercial toward retention and satisfaction).

When the chatbot fails to understand or solve a problem, acknowledge the misunderstanding and offer a recovery path; clarification requests raise perceived anthropomorphism and adoption intent, and users prefer repair that acknowledges the breakdown and suggests solutions.

Accompany recommendations, instructions, or unexpected information with explanations or justifications; justification and rapport-building raise trust, perceived transparency, satisfaction, usefulness, and ease of use, and are especially relevant for customer-service and recommendation chatbots.

Apply naturalness practices - self-introduction, a welcoming opening that states capabilities and optionally collects the user's name, addressing the user by name, small talk, echoing user responses, casual language, and humanization techniques such as adaptive response speed - to raise perceived anthropomorphism and social presence and reduce user resistance; naturalness is the baseline for every chatbot.

Combine politeness with restrained informality rather than either extreme, adjust language features to the domain, and keep informality from undermining the chatbot's professional image; informal elements build closeness and motivation more in health and learning contexts than in commercial ones, and warm, polite openers raise engagement.

Use typing cues and slightly delayed responses to make the chatbot feel less instantaneous and more human - raising perceived humanness, social presence, and satisfaction - but balance them against task efficiency.
Pretest how target users perceive intended practices, because user belief about the chatbot determines impact more than the designer's intended identity or effect.
Let the chatbot's purpose drive the desired user relationship, the target impacts, and the primary conversational-design focus.

Tune emphasis to purpose: information-collection and transaction chatbots state capabilities and limitations early; information and recommendation chatbots emphasize credibility and trust (recommendation also intimacy-building); well-being chatbots emphasize companionship, intimacy, and encouragement.

Treat naturalness as the baseline for every chatbot, and foreground transparency when competent task performance matters most and emotionality when deeper user connection matters most, deciding explicitly which to foreground since they can coexist.

Avoid repetitive or identical messages, exaggerated practice use, hidden chatbot identity, machine-like typefaces such as OCR-A, and intentional or forced typing errors, which reduce perceived humanness and can read as developer incompetence.
Keep only conversational practices that are pragmatic, replicable, and backed by concrete implementation examples; translate broad subjective characteristics into implementable behavior or drop them.
Author multiple varied formulations for each recurring communicative function so repeated use of a practice does not make the chatbot feel machine-like.

Base conversational guidance on primary, full research studies that measure user-centered outcomes such as satisfaction and trust, excluding studies that report no user impact or only algorithmic or technical performance, and passing each study through a quality checklist.

Do not treat avatars as context-independent improvements: avatar gender and appearance shape user impressions before any message, effects are inconsistent across studies, human-like avatars raise expectations and frustration after failures, and auto-activation can worsen anthropomorphic avatars - pair avatar choices with transparency and failure handling, and test them.

Account for interactions between practices - avatar activation mode, humor style, limitation acknowledgement, disclosure timing, and pretending to be human - rather than treating each practice in isolation.

Design how the conversation is initiated: a system-initiated, non-anthropomorphic assistant can raise user reactance and auto-activated agents can fare worse with anthropomorphic avatars, so prefer user-initiated openings or carefully designed onboarding.

Use emotionality practices - exclamatory feedback, graphical media (emoji, emoticons, GIFs, memes), a social-oriented informal style, and humor - to raise social presence and positive perceptions such as enjoyment, credibility, engagement, and behavioral intentions.

Convey empathy by adapting responses to what the user said, acknowledging negative situations, restating the user's message, and using active listening (paraphrasing, verbalizing emotions, summarizing, encouraging); sentiment-adaptive and supportive messages raise perceived empathy, valence, and engagement.

When disclosing non-human identity, pair it with explicit capability statements and limitations, and accept the resulting drop in perceived humanness because transparency prevents the greater harm of perceived deception.

Use buttons, carousels, preset options, and mixed-modality inputs to streamline input and reduce breakdowns, but cautiously, because they reduce perceived humanness and social presence even when satisfaction is unaffected (they can aid task understanding and enjoyability).
Account for user moderators - demographics, personality, language proficiency, technology experience, conversation duration, and usage context - because they change a practice's impact.

When target-user testing is not feasible, avoid exaggerated use of any conversational practice; over-use can backfire - heavy socio-emotional features can reduce users' willingness to disclose data, and persuasive inquiry can lower donation probability.

Deliver guidance in simple, objective, and clear language with short explanations, concrete per-practice examples, extended before-and-after examples, and references to supporting studies; state the objective and scope or limitations early and do not present it as exhaustive or as a full technical or process manual.
Apply transparency practices - presenting capabilities, acknowledging limitations, making suggestions, and asking for clarification - to support competent task performance and adoption.

Mirror the user's language and comply with the domain register: lexical and structural alignment raises user alignment, register compliance raises perceived appropriateness and credibility, and code-mixing can raise perceived conversational ability and humanness - moderated by the user's language proficiency.
Design the interaction sequence as a first-class object, not just the language recognizer, response text, or visual shell.
Design conversational interfaces as ordered utterance sequences grounded in human conversation, not as visual-control layouts with text attached.
Set expectations and scope around the agent as a constrained conversational simulation rather than a human-equivalent interlocutor.
Use natural conversation as the interaction metaphor and mutual understanding as the success criterion for agent-user exchanges.
Use transcript-level inspection to evaluate what the interaction actually does turn by turn, and include embodied or setting context when that context affects interpretation.
Use elicitation, repeat, and paraphrase techniques to display hearing and invite elaboration, while treating them as limited interactional displays rather than proof of deep understanding.
Use a content schema with separate slots for user utterance, agent utterance, repeat, paraphrase, example, and definition.
Avoid a two-turn valid-query model when users need to build on prior turns; preserve sequential context so follow-ups, references, repair, and closings have an interactional target.
For conversational delivery, answer the user's immediate need first and expose contingencies or additional details through shorter follow-up chunks.
Model intents around the conversational action the user is performing, not only around the domain topic mentioned.
Do not automatically take the next turn after every answer; leave third position available for the user to close, repair, accept, reject, or otherwise respond.
Implement conversation-management actions as core agent capabilities, including preliminaries, repair requests, acknowledgments, cancellations, sequence closings, and conversation closings.
Organize a conversational pattern library into primary activities, sequence-level management, and conversation-level management.
Model primary conversational activities with reusable modules for inquiries, requests, extended tellings, known-answer questions, and information capture.
Include conversation-lifecycle patterns for openings, capability and topic negotiation, transitions, last-topic checks, closings, and disengagement.
Design conversation-centric flows as mixed-initiative and nonlinear so either party can lead and the user can redirect the trajectory.
Use a systematic conversation-analysis framework, such as NCF, to compensate for platform gaps in modeling turn-by-turn interaction.
Build the core experience so it works through words alone, then add visual aids only as progressive enhancement for channels that support them.
Treat interaction-style categories as design diagnostics, not rigid boxes; mix styles deliberately when the application benefits from more than one.
Evaluate understanding by demonstrated performance across probing, varied situations, not by the mere ability to continue a conversation or claim comprehension.
Scope claims of machine understanding to narrow, practical domains unless performance holds up under varied probing and phrasing.
In ordinary interaction, assume understanding provisionally and repair when trouble appears instead of probing every expression for exact meaning.
Pair NLU with natural conversation understanding by testing interpretations in interaction and repairing misunderstandings or partial understandings when they surface.
Expose the agent's interpretation of the user's utterance, action, or topic when that interpretation affects the next move, so the user can repair it if needed.
Apply recipient design, minimization, and repair together when writing automated-agent utterances.
Compose conversational-activity modules into larger workflows instead of designing each complex activity from scratch.
Provide sequence-management behavior for misunderstanding, hearing trouble, successful completion, and user aborts.
Treat post-answer user turns as operational feedback about whether the prior sequence succeeded, needs repair, or should be abandoned.
Capture multiple variants of the same user action for training and allow agent response variants when response selection needs sequence or randomness.
Pre-author repair content so the agent can repeat, restate, exemplify, or define its prior response when users ask for help understanding it.
Use paraphrase as a scoped repair: elaborate when the primary answer is short and context-poor, but shorten to the upshot when the primary answer is long or confusing.
For stories, instructions, or other long agent tellings, split content into interactive parts that advance through pauses or user continuers.
Begin UX work by asking the framing questions that clarify user and product issues before choosing methods, technologies, or implementation details.
Elicit requirements from users and stakeholders, then probe proposed solutions to find the underlying needs and impediments.
Use a shared UX vocabulary and the five-plane model to make design concerns discussable across the team.
Shape user-facing form around user psychology, behavior, task context, and surrounding controls rather than around internal functionality alone.
Increase explicit UX design attention as product features, functions, or usage steps add complexity.
Define product strategy explicitly around what the organization wants and what users want before design execution begins.
Design web and multi-screen products as self-service experiences that help users understand what to do without making them feel incapable.
Connect UX decisions to business and organizational outcomes such as loyalty, conversion, efficiency, employee productivity, and satisfaction.
Respect the dependency chain from strategy through surface while allowing later-plane discoveries to trigger lower-plane reevaluation before work is finalized.
Analyze hybrid products through both task/functionality concerns and information/meaning concerns instead of forcing them into one category.
Build categorization from product objectives, user needs, and actual content or functionality by balancing top-down strategy with bottom-up requirements analysis.
Assign attention to every UX element without assuming every element needs its own specialist.
Treat content and technology as experience-shaping constraints and assets during UX planning.
Translate strategy into scope by defining content and functionality requirements that expose conflicts, reduce ambiguity, and guide feature evaluation.
Choose success metrics that tie to design-influenceable user behavior and interpret them in strategic and external context.
Segment users only where shared characteristics reveal distinct needs, and revise segments as research improves understanding.
Select research methods according to the type and depth of understanding needed, with awareness of participant-depth trade-offs.
Actively manage scope by moving useful out-of-scope ideas into future-release planning instead of letting them expand the current milestone.
Scope functionality and content together because each can create requirements for the other.
After scope is prioritized, define structure as the cohesive arrangement of options and sequences grounded in how users think and behave.
Write requirements as positive, specific, objective, and falsifiable statements of intended behavior.
Prioritize requirements by strategic fit, user-need fit, and implementation feasibility.
Prefer interaction structures that work for users over those that are merely technically efficient.
At the skeleton level, diagnose whether a problem is about action, movement, or communication before choosing an interface, navigation, or information-design solution.
Design interfaces around likely user tasks by choosing understandable controls, emphasizing important elements, reducing unneeded elements, and avoiding rare-edge-case dominance.
Choose defaults, persistence, and controls as explicit trade-offs among user goals, implementation complexity, screen space, option visibility, and user effort.
Design navigation to support real movement, explain relationships among options, and show how options relate to the current page.
Provide wayfinding cues that clarify current location, available destinations, and goal-supporting paths, with visual cues reinforcing rather than replacing other location signals.
Use wireframes to integrate page components across interface, navigation, and information design, with annotations where layout alone is ambiguous.
Evaluate surface and visual design by how well sensory presentation supports lower-plane objectives, structure, brand intent, and attention hierarchy.
Shape visual flow so attention moves smoothly through goal-supporting possibilities, using informal attention checks when sufficient and more precise methods when needed.
Use contrast and uniformity deliberately so important distinctions, relationships, and groups are noticeable without creating confusion.
Build visual systems from reusable recurring elements, grids, and standards, but revisit those standards when they no longer fit product needs.
Maintain external visual consistency across media when a coherent organizational brand impression matters.
Define color and typography systems that balance emphasis, readability, meaningful distinction, consistency, and restraint.
Use design comps to test whether visual components form a cohesive whole while preserving the wireframe's relative importance and grouping.
Scale UX staffing and process to product complexity while ensuring every plane is covered, whether by specialists or a synchronized small team.
For each UX issue, identify the real problem and plane, then evaluate solution consequences across the whole plane stack.
Reject design decisions driven by default technology structure, unexamined mimicry, or authority preference; require a user-and-strategy answer for why the decision exists.
Adapt UX methods to constraints with lighter-weight evidence when necessary, but do not postpone fundamental UX learning until it is too late to act.
Plan development as alternating periods of fast production and deliberate reflection, protecting strategy, scope, and structure work because it saves time later.

Protect both lower-plane foundations and upper-plane execution: surface or skeleton polish cannot compensate for weak strategy, scope, or structure, and upper-plane failures can hide sound lower-plane decisions.
